title: Man shot, handcuffed; Amherstburg police sent to wrong address, inquest told
article: Robert Scott Carpenter was handcuffed after being shot by an Amherstburg police officer and suffered multiple "blunt force" injuries shortly before he died, a coroner's jury heard Tuesday.
The jury also heard three Amherstburg police officers were dispatched to the wrong address after receiving a disrupted 911 call from Carpenter's 258 McCurdy Dr. home.
Carpenter, 36, was shot by Amherstburg police Const. Shawn McCurdy shortly after 7 a.m. last Oct. 30, Coroner's Counsel Robert Ash told the jury.
Efforts to revive him failed and Carpenter died on the operating table from complications brought on by a single-bullet wound to his upper right leg.
The chain of events began with a disrupted 911 call made by Lisa Stewart, Carpenter's common-law-wife.
Ash said that the call was made because Stewart feared "possible injuries" due to Carpenter's erratic behaviour.
That behaviour included strapping a hunting knife to his belt and insisting the air and water in his house were poisoned.
The call was routed to the 911 centre in North Bay and Amherstburg police were dispatched to the wrong address. Carpenter had obtained a new phone number just days before the incident.

When the error was realized, McCurdy and Sgt. Bart DiPasquale left the Amherstburg police station and drove the short distance to Carpenter's home. DiPasquale was off-duty, out of uniform and without his police-service revolver, said Ash. He made the drive in his private vehicle.
After a scuffle that saw McCurdy pull Stewart from the house and Carpenter allegedly shove him, McCurdy was joined on the porch by DiPasquale and another officer, said Ash.

DiPasquale fell forward when the door suddenly opened and was attacked by a knife-wielding Carpenter, said Ash. When Carpenter refused to stop, said Ash, McCurdy fired a single shot from his service revolver -- a .40 calibre Smith and Wesson.
David Klodt, a forensics expert with the civilian agency that probed the shooting, said no tests were undertaken to determine the cause of DiPasquale's minor injuries.
Under cross-examination by Patrick Ducharme, lawyer for the Carpenters, Klodt said the knife allegedly used in the assault was only recently sent for analysis.
Pathologist Anthony Allevato said it was possible DiPasquale's injuries were caused by fingernails, a broken hall mirror or a knife.

A June 16 Windsor Star article reported Stewart's claim that Carpenter never attacked an officer with a knife. Citing the article andrew Bradie, lawyer for the officers involved in the shooting, requested a Star reporter be subpoenaed by the inquest. Regional Coroner Tom Wilson said witnesses could be cross-examined on published reports but reserved his decision on the subpoena request.
Klodt said no gunshot residue tests were performed because the officers involved were in close proximity.
When Ducharme asked Klodt if he was aware of another gun registered to DiPasquale, Klodt said he was not.
Despite his injuries, said Ash, Carpenter continued to struggle with police and was handcuffed and carried outside.
When they realized he was injured, police removed the handcuffs.

Allevato testified the bullet entered near Carpenter's lower pelvis and travelled downward from left to right at a 45-degree angle. Entering from the front, the bullet completely severed the right femoral vein.

Allevato said it would have been possible for Carpenter to put up a struggle but that his injuries would have immobilized him. The bullet fractured Carpenter's leg, causing it to shorten and externally rotate.
Allevato said Carpenter suffered a "number of blunt force injuries" including three "good-sized bruises" to the back of his head, a bruised forehead and bruises on his chest and neck.
